extracted.intended_audience: Benefit Control Officers (BCOs), Agent IIs, District Managers, UIC administrators, and legal practitioners involved in unemployment insurance enforcement and appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for deciding between administrative penalties and criminal prosecution under the Unemployment Insurance Act, calculating and recovering penalties, preparing prosecution files, and the structure and procedure of appeals (Board of Referees, Umpire, Federal Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between administrative penalties and criminal prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative penalties provided for under sec. 47 become applicable only 'where there are mitigating or extenuating circumstances'; criminal sanctions would therefore appear to be the rule and administrative penalties a departure from the norm for the benefit of claimants whose responsibility seems extenuated by their own particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs should recommend administrative penalties instead of prosecution when the claimant's personal circumstances make prosecution unduly severe; Agents II weigh the BCO's recommendation but make the final decision. Examples of mitigating circumstances that may justify recourse to sec. 47 include health, financial or family reasons and 'good' motives (e.g., obtaining money to pay large medical expenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty amount ceiling and parity with court fines
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of the penalty must not exceed the average fines imposed by the courts for a comparable number of similar offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines emphasize uniformity and that administrative penalties should not be more severe than criminal court fines for comparable offences; Agent IIs must seek District Manager approval for any penalty above $500. Although the Act allows up to three times the weekly rate per false statement, the guidelines set lower practical ceilings (see penalty calculation methodology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating circumstances (UIC Manual list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating circumstances listed in the UIC Manual (sec. 501.3.7) include: the claimant's lack of knowledge of some obligations; a mistake resulting from inaccurate information provided by an officer of the UIC; the state of his health at relevant times; age (very young or very old); an advanced state of pregnancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases of misinformation by a UIC officer, the UIC may refrain from imposing any sanction. The BCO must bring such extenuating circumstances to the Agent II's attention and may recommend less severe penalties or none at all (reimbursement only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claimant's motives and personal circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent II must appraise the motives of the author of the false statement and take into account motives such as ensuring material security for family under difficult circumstances; a 'good' motive might constitute mitigating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claimant's real intention was not to defraud but to secure basic needs, the Agent II may forego penalties and require only reimbursement. BCOs must indicate motives in their reports; Agents II should consider them when moderating recommended penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of reputation and employment consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Resort should be had to Section 47 instead of prosecution whenever, as a result of the claimant's personal circumstances, the effect of prosecution would be more severe than is desired (e.g., protecting reputations of very young/old claimants; avoiding loss of present job or impediment to return to particular field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs are advised against recommending prosecution if it would cause job loss or impede return to employment, except where the claimant's job requires a high degree of honesty and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and cost of witnesses; deterrence and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative penalties may be used even though the seriousness of the violation would justify prosecution when there is doubt about availability of essential witnesses or when the cost of having them appear would be disproportionately high; however, officers should not avoid prosecution merely to save time and money if guilt could be conclusively proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed to prosecution despite apparent excessive costs where prosecution will have a deterrent effect, will substantially correct a critical violation situation, or a large number of flagrant offences are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCO reporting requirements when recommending penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The BCO must justify his recommendation, bring to light all factors likely to influence the Agent II's decision, indicate any extenuating circumstances, and establish the extent to which the claimant was aware of the false or misleading nature of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quality and completeness of the BCO's file/interview report directly affect the Agent II's ability to decide; BCOs should document motives, awareness, evidence and any mitigating facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent II decision-making authority and supervisory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agent II decides whether to impose a penalty and its amount on the basis of the BCO's information; in principle he will impose a penalty only if the BCO recommends it, but he may moderate or decide against imposition. His autonomy is limited by guidelines and he must obtain District Manager approval for any penalty above $500.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agent IIs should adhere to uniform criteria; deviations from guideline rules to reduce a penalty require express authorization of the District Manager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of deliberate intent and flagrancy
rubrics_metrics.description: In weighing whether the claimant acted in bad faith, the Agent II must consider admissions, witness evidence, or the claimant's possession of or access to necessary documents; the flagrancy of distortion of facts indicates deliberate intent rather than lack of knowledge or negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deliberate intent is clear (e.g., concealment of regular full salary), treat more severely; occasional small omissions warrant lighter treatment. The amount and regularity of undisclosed earnings should be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty calculation methodology (light/medium/heavy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines distinguish light, medium and heavy penalties: light for not more than three offences; medium for four or five offences; heavy for six or more offences. Penalties are calculated by multiplying: one quarter of the claimant's weekly benefit rate for a light penalty; half the weekly benefit rate for a medium penalty; the weekly benefit rate for a heavy penalty; by the number of offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules may be broken only to reduce the penalty (with District Manager authorization). The guidelines set the maximum penalty per false statement at one week of benefits even though the Act allows up to three times the weekly rate; uniformity is stressed so penalties generally stay well below the statutory maximum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of penalties as debts and recovery procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts imposed as penalties under sec. 47 are a debt due to Her Majesty recoverable like benefits; recovery time limit for administrative penalties is extended up to 72 months (sec. 49(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery procedures are identical to those for overpayments (certification of debts, registration, garnishment). Penalties may be deducted from benefits payable to the same claimant or written off if recovery imposes undue hardship (sec. 58(1) and reg. 175).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory offence categories under the Act (sec. 121, 122, 123, 128)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act defines offences including: false or misleading statements made knowingly in relation to a claim for benefit; furnishing false information required by the Act/Regulations; obtaining benefit by false pretences; non-disclosure that results in a false application; negotiating a cheque for benefits one knows one is not entitled to; failure to return cheques as required by sec. 50. Employer offences (sec. 122) prohibit false/misleading statements/returns about employment/earnings and can attract fines and orders to pay double overpayments. Sec. 128 prohibits fraudulent SIN applications, fraudulent use of another's SIN, and counterfeiting SIN cards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These offences generally require a mental/intentional element (knowledge of fraudulent nature). Specific sanctions range (e.g., sec. 124 residual sanction: max fine $500 or up to six months imprisonment; SIN offences: max fine $1,000 or up to one year imprisonment; employer fines between $25 and $5,000 and possible double payment orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and criminal procedure for prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutions under the Unemployment Insurance Act must be laid within five years from the date of the action referred to in the charge (cf. sec. 83(4) applied by sec. 111(1)). The procedure applicable is that specified in Part XXIV of the Criminal Code (summary conviction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BCOs and supervisors must be aware of limitation periods and follow summary conviction procedure requirements when drafting complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCO reporting requirements when recommending prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: When recommending prosecution the BCO's report must be drafted with special care: it must give an accurate account of the facts established, and of the evidence supporting each fact, with particular attention to the intentional aspect of the offence and notation of claimant's motives that may mitigate responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poorly drafted report undermines prosecution; the report supports supervisory and legal review and the prima facie case assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution approval process and procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation for prosecution is referred to the Benefit Control supervisor, who examines the interview report and, if persisted, forwards the file to the District Manager. District Managers may delegate authority to Benefit Control supervisors. The Regional Chief of Benefit Control solicits the opinion of Regional Legal Counsel whose approval is required before prosecution can be initiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Regional Legal Counsel and regional Benefit Control concur on evidence sufficiency and policy fit, the supervisor drafts the summary (complaint), lays the complaint, liaises with UIC legal services, ensures the investigating BCO is available to testify, follows the case to conclusion, and drafts a press release explaining the prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent administrative appeals and prosecution; court deferral (sec. 118)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a danger of the claimant being tried criminally and then later having eligibility recognized by the Umpire. Sec. 118 attempts to circumvent this by requiring the courts to defer their decision when a prosecution raises a question that has yet to be finally settled by the Commission or by the appeal tribunals with jurisdiction in matters involving benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice courts sometimes disregard sec. 118; if the court does not take note and the accused fails to invoke it, it is the responsibility of the UIC to remind the courts of its existence (as noted in CUB 3752).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal review and contentious review pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal review exists under sec. 102 when the claimant presents new facts in support of a review; a claimant who merely disagrees may request reconsideration but the Agent's decision remains his alone until contentious review is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contentious review has two degrees: initial review by the Board of Referees (secs. 56,91,94,102; regs. 167,178–182) and second-level review by the Umpire (secs. 92–100; regs. 167,183–186). A third level exists via Federal Court judicial review (recognized by sec. 100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and formation of the Board of Referees
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board of Referees is composed of a chairman and at least two members divided evenly between 'employers or representatives of employers' and 'insured persons or representatives of insured persons'; chairmen are appointed by the Governor in Council and other members by the UIC. The Board is constituted afresh each time an appeal is lodged from panels of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tripartite composition is intended to legitimize administrative action and provide public participation; because the Board is reconstituted for each appeal, it ceases to exist once a decision is handed down, which has procedural consequences when a case is resubmitted.
